newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade bourse turnover up in week to March 7.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade bourse turnover up in week to March 7.

text.p: The Belgrade Stock Exchange (BSE) reported on Monday a 7.19 percent rise in its turnover during the week ending March 7, despite tightening liquidity in the banking sector.
Total turnover rose to 34.46 million dinars ($6.07 million) in 213 deals from 32.148 million in 192 deals a week ago.
Traders said the liquidity of the banking sector deteriorated on Friday, with banks withdrawing funds from the market and getting ready for the announced pension payouts last Saturday.

An unexpected decision by the central bank to apply the 15 percent reserve requirement not only to banks' deposits but also to their interbank lending was another reason for the banks to withdraw funds from the market.

Coupled with the latest Serbian government regulation to introduce a 10 percent tax on all credit deals with interest rates exceeding the discount rate by more than 30 percent, the measure simply forced banks to pull out, analysts said.
"This has already led to a sizeable contraction in the interbank market volume and will definitely stifle activity on this market in the months ahead," an analyst told Reuters.
The unofficial interbank market, also called the giro money market, serves banks to trade their surplus liquidity and is the shortest way to borrow and bridge short-term illiquidity.
But banks were seen searching for new forms of doing business with each other, which analysts feared could lead to a flood of various securities coming to the market.

"Unlike giro money, trade in securities is not taxed and banks are inventive enough to find their way out. But with such securities booming, we could face a dramatic deterioration in the quality and security of an investment," the analyst said.
The National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) decision last week to cut its key discount rate to 2.5 from 4.5 percent per month did not have much effect on the market activity, traders said.
"The lower discount rate only means the NBY has given in to pressures by the powerful debtor lobby," a trader told Reuters.
Analysts criticised the central bank discount rate policy for being inconsistent. "It does not influence other interest rates nor does it reflect true movements in inflation," an analyst said.
For the week ending March 7, the BSE reported the following details:
* Commercial paper traded 193 times for a total of 31.853 million dinars.
* There were 18 deals in treasury bills worth 2.474 million dinars.
Interest rates on commercial paper and treasury bills ranged between an annual 331 and 520 percent and maturity stood between one and 30 days.
*The BSE reported no deals in the central bank short-term bonds and wheat contracts.

"The bonds, launched as an instrument to regulate banks' liquidity, became unnecessary after the 15 percent reserve requirement was introduced. NBY hardly sells any of the bonds it auctions once a month on the bourse anyway," a trader said.
*OTC trade in commercial paper and treasury bills stood at 22.103 million dinars, down on 24.382 million a week ago.
*OTC trade in the giro money market fell to 13.27 million from 20.00 million dinars.
-- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
($1 = 5.6694 Yugoslav dinars)
